title: Labeling for Health: Impact of a Percent Daily Value Traffic Light System on Food Choices in a University Food Pantry
content: Background/Objectives: Food insecurity disproportionately affects college students, particularly those from low-income and ethnically diverse backgrounds. Limited access to nutrition education and culturally relevant food options exacerbates poor dietary habits. This study evaluated a nutrition education intervention combined with a Percent Daily Value (%DV)-based traffic light labeling system on improving dietary behavior and nutrient intake among college students using a university food pantry at a Hispanic-serving institution. Methods: In this randomized controlled trial, 67 students were assigned to either an experimental (n = 36) or control (n = 31) group. Both groups participated in a 3-week intervention: the experimental group received nutrition education with traffic-light labeling in the pantry’s online ordering platform, while the control group received general campus resources. Pre- and post-intervention dietary intake was assessed using ASA24® dietary recalls. Nutrient intakes were compared to the Dietary Reference Intakes (DRIs) to assess adequacy. Results: Post-intervention, the experimental group showed a statistically significant decrease in red-labeled food selections (p = 0.02) and a reduction in saturated fat intake (p = 0.04). However, no significant differences were found between groups in overall nutrient intake. The percentage of participants meeting DRI recommendations increased modestly across most nutrients in both groups; however, group-wise differences were not statistically significant. Conclusions: This intervention showed promise in improving food selection behaviors among food-insecure students, though its effect on overall nutrient adequacy was limited. Future studies should combine labeling strategies with longer, interactive education formats and improved pantry offerings to enhance dietary quality among diverse college populations.
